content: For-profit NGOs, such as charities and faith-based organizations, often initiate services in low-income settings where public or private services fail to meet evident needs. These NGOs adopt a social approach similar to social enterprises, frequently offering services free of charge or at subsidized rates. Their operations are typically funded through private donations, philanthropic contributions, corporate social responsibility initiatives, or, in some cases, government or insurance funds. However, these services are often project-based, making them vulnerable to funding cuts. Like other entities, NGOs must adhere to state regulations. Prosthetics and orthotics services are optimally positioned within the health ministry and should be integrated into the national healthcare system. This integration ensures specialized health services address a variety of health conditions, improving health outcomes and advancing universal health coverage. These services are typically provided in collaboration with other health services, such as surgery and rehabilitation, emphasizing the importance of close linkages for optimal outcomes. Additionally, these services can reduce overall healthcare costs. Prosthetics and orthotics services often require medical interventions, such as wound healing, X-rays, surgery, and therapy. The entry point for these services is frequently general health services. For instance, prosthetic fittings are necessary after amputations, orthoses are required following surgeries or paralysis, and diabetic conditions often necessitate specialized footwear. Many users of these services are hospital inpatients or recently discharged patients. Providers of prosthetics and orthotics services, regardless of their affiliation, should collaborate with hospital departments, including orthopedics, rehabilitation, neurology, pediatrics, geriatrics, and emergency services. When these services are not located within the same facility, providers can maintain contact through consultations in hospitals and clinics. Collaboration with decentralized health services, such as district hospitals and community health programs, is crucial for identifying, referring, and following up with users. This integration strengthens the continuum of care and expands the range of available services, ensuring early identification and treatment of conditions requiring prosthetics and orthotics interventions. The inclusion of prosthetics and orthotics services in the health sector promotes inclusive healthcare for all, including individuals with disabilities. It reinforces the continuum of care, encompassing preventive, promotive, curative, rehabilitative, assistive, and palliative interventions. While the health ministry typically leads these services, other sectors, such as education, economic empowerment, and social integration, also play significant roles. Strong links between health, education, employment, and social sectors are essential. The distribution of prosthetics and orthotics services should align with the population's needs and distribution. Most countries require multiple service units of varying capacities at different levels and locations. Ideally, all units should provide a comprehensive range of services. However, in resource-limited settings, this may not be feasible due to the need for specialized personnel and facilities for rare and complex cases. Responsibilities can be distributed across different service levels, ensuring a wide range of services is available as close as possible to users. A three-level service delivery system, integrated within the broader healthcare system, can organize prosthetics and orthotics services. At the primary level, services can extend from an exclusive prosthetics and orthotics approach to an integrated approach involving other health and rehabilitation sectors. This includes identification, referral, follow-up, and basic treatments. At the secondary level, standard units provide commonly required treatments and maintain links with tertiary services for complex cases. Tertiary centers offer specialized services, often serving as centers of excellence for national or regional leadership, research, and training. These centers should provide a wide range of technologies and have access to inpatient rehabilitation beds for complex cases. After treatment at secondary or tertiary levels, users can be followed up at the primary level, close to their homes. Technical support and monitoring are essential throughout the system to maintain high-quality services, particularly at the primary level, where personnel may have less specialized training. Decentralization of prosthetics and orthotics services is crucial for reaching remote and rural areas. Service units can act as hubs for decentralized services through satellite units, mobile units, outreach services, or community program linkages. Each approach has advantages and disadvantages, such as varying levels of service quality and cost-effectiveness. Decentralized services must be closely monitored to ensure treatment and product quality. While decentralization incurs additional costs for service providers, it can result in significant savings for users, making it economically justifiable. In many countries, decentralization is the only viable way to reach all individuals in need. Advanced treatment needs identified in decentralized services can be referred to appropriate levels within the service system. In countries with effective public or private insurance coverage, private prosthetics and orthotics service providers often align their distribution with service demand. These providers have a financial incentive to establish appropriately sized and specialized units in favorable business environments. Private services may operate as standalone units or as part of enterprises with branches in various cities. While collaboration with other providers may be limited, private providers have a strong financial incentive to work with the health sector, increasing client numbers and income.
